summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor to Wyoming, because Wyoming stands under the United States federal framework. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to correct the misapplication of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad; the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Facilities access inside Wyoming is restricted by statute. On Monday, 3 March 2025, Governor Mark Gordon signed two measures into law. House Bill 72, the Protecting Privacy in Public Spaces Act, covers sex-designated restrooms, showers, sleeping quarters and locker rooms at public facilities. Senate File 62, Sex-Designated Facilities and Public Schools, requires public school children from pre-kindergarten upward, including charter school students, to use restrooms aligned with sex assigned at birth; districts must provide a reasonable accommodation to any student who does not wish to use a multiple-occupancy restroom or locker room matching the gender at that student's birth. The Movement Advancement Project equality map records these Wyoming facility bans alongside the year of enactment.

A national legal-risk assessment published in July 2026 lists Wyoming among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults. The assessment draws on five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric identifying the most severe bills, and it was republished on 27 August 2026 by a regional LGBTQ outlet. The same assessment records federal policies that continue to generate legal difficulty for transgender people across the country.
tangentialFactors:
The federal layer constrains care and screening regardless of state. Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as chemical and surgical mutilation of children, leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed records for patients under 19 from more than 20 hospitals, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and several federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

Screening at United States checkpoints carries an outing risk: TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the country to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban on fraud grounds. Several foreign governments responded: in April 2025 CNN reported that multiple countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.

Wyoming's March 2025 statutes sit within a wider facilities picture. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other states. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest Do Not Travel state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged.
localsOnly:
For Wyoming residents, the operative rules are House Bill 72 and Senate File 62, both signed 3 March 2025. House Bill 72 governs sex-designated restrooms, showers, sleeping quarters and locker rooms at public facilities. Senate File 62 governs public schools, charter schools included, from pre-kindergarten upward, and requires districts to offer a reasonable accommodation to a student who declines to use a multiple-occupancy restroom or locker room matching the gender at that student's birth.

Residents are also subject to the federal document regime: passports and other federal identity documents are issued only as M or F according to supporting records, and the X marker is no longer processed. Existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiry. The Federal Bureau of Prisons has adopted policies mandating conversion-therapy-style measures for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting radical gender ideology and characterised as domestic terrorist groups, and a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist. Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not state penalties, enforcement mechanisms or any arrests under Wyoming House Bill 72 or Senate File 62, so the practical consequences of breaching the facility rules remain unresolved.

No Wyoming-specific rule on changing birth-certificate or driver's-licence sex markers is sourced here; the Kansas statute cited is a separate state's law and should not be read as Wyoming's. Whether Wyoming has enacted comparable document restrictions is not established by this inventory.

The July 2026 legal-risk assessment's underlying rubric and bill-by-bill scores are not reproduced in the available material, so the basis for ranking Wyoming among the worst states cannot be verified directly; only its methodology description and republication date are sourced.

It is unresolved whether the court injunctions affecting various federal measures apply to any specific federal action a visitor to Wyoming might encounter, and the sources do not indicate whether the reasonable-acmodation clause of Senate File 62 is used in practice by Wyoming school districts.
